title: Learning University Mathematics through the Algebra of Bookkeeping
text:
Preface
This book teaches university mathematics through one running example: double-entry bookkeeping. Each part takes the same small set of business transactions and describes them again in a new mathematical language. Sets and maps come first, then monoids and groups, vector spaces, graphs, and categories. The main theorems are formalized in Lean 4, so a reader can check them by machine.
The book does not assume any knowledge of bookkeeping. It assumes high-school mathematics.

title: Learning University Mathematics through the Algebra of Bookkeeping
text:
Why Part 0 comes first
Before any mathematics, Part 0 shows how the material in this book was found. It treats “the algebra of bookkeeping” as a research topic and walks through the search that produced this book’s bibliography: the queries, the databases, the tools that worked, and the tools that failed. Every search reported in Part 0 was carried out on 15 October 2026, and the results describe what the tools returned on that day. Search results change over time, so a reader who repeats a search should expect different numbers.

title: Learning University Mathematics through the Algebra of Bookkeeping
text:
A rule this book follows
Every factual claim in this book is checked against a source before it is written down, and a claim that cannot be checked is left out. Bibliographic data was checked against Crossref, arXiv, CiNii Research, Internet Archive catalog records, publishers’ pages, or the papers themselves.

title: Part 0: Research Methods
text:
The rest of this book teaches mathematics through bookkeeping. Part 0 comes first because it answers a question a careful reader will ask: where does this material come from, and how do we know it is right?
Part 0 follows one literature search from start to finish. The topic is the algebra of bookkeeping itself, so the papers it finds are the sources of the later parts. 1  Asking a Researchable Question to 7  Reading Papers show how to find and read those sources. 8  Organizing What You Find and 10  Writing Up the Survey show how to record them and summarize them. 9  Limits and Pitfalls collects the places where tools, records, and our own drafts went wrong.
Each chapter ends with exercises that apply the same steps to a topic of your choice. A reader who wants to start the mathematics at once can go to Part I and come back to Part 0 when a later chapter cites a source.

title: 1  Asking a Researchable Question
text:
1.1 From an interest to questions
Every search starts from a question. A vague question produces a vague search, so the first task is to turn a loose interest into questions that a database can answer.
This book began with a loose interest: what is double-entry bookkeeping, mathematically? A database cannot answer that sentence directly. Looking back at our search, it answered the following smaller questions, each of which names something a database can find. Writing such questions down at the start, as we recommend here, makes the search easier to plan.
Each question points to a branch of mathematics, and each branch has its own vocabulary. Chapter 2 turns these questions into search terms.

title: 1  Asking a Researchable Question
text:
Has anyone described double-entry bookkeeping as an algebraic structure, such as a group or a monoid?
Has anyone written bookkeeping with matrices or vectors?
Has anyone described bookkeeping as a graph or a network?
Has anyone used category theory for bookkeeping?
Has anyone stated axioms for accounting measurement?
When did these ideas appear, and who wrote them first?

title: 1  Asking a Researchable Question
text:
1.2 Deciding the scope
A question also needs boundaries. Our search had four.

Fields. The work could come from accounting, mathematics, computer science, or economics. We kept all four in scope, because a paper on “ledgers” in computer science may answer the same question as a paper on “accounts” in accounting.
Languages. We searched in English and in Japanese. Part of the literature on this topic is written in Japanese (Chapter 5).
Time. We set no lower limit on the publication year. According to Ellerman (2014), the double-entry method was in business use for over five centuries, and the oldest work in this book’s bibliography dates from 1880 (Chapter 6).
Kind of source. We accepted journal articles, preprints, books, and university repository papers. We excluded copies of works posted by sites that are not the publisher or the author (Chapter 9).

title: 1  Asking a Researchable Question
text:
1.3 Writing the question down
Write the question and the scope in a research log before your first search. The log is a plain text file with dates. Each search later adds an entry: the date, the tool, the exact query, and what came back. The worked examples in this part describe searches we ran on 15 October 2026.

title: 2  Collecting Keywords
text:
2.1 Each field has its own name for the idea
A search engine matches words. If the authors of a paper used a different word from yours, the search misses the paper. This chapter shows how we collected the words that authors in this field use.
The same idea appears under different names in different fields. These are the names we found in titles and abstracts during our search:
Two lessons follow from this table.
First, the name of a mathematical structure can be a sharper search term than the name of the subject. The abstract of Ellerman (2014) introduces the name “Pacioli group” for the group of differences used in bookkeeping, so the term points to this line of work.
Second, the historical Italian name partita doppia is the title of a category theory paper (Katis et al. 2008). Its title does not contain the English words “double-entry bookkeeping,” so a search restricted to titles in English would miss it. In our search it appeared in response to a Google Scholar query that combined “double-entry,” “bookkeeping,” and “category theory.”

title: 2  Collecting Keywords
text:
2.2 Where the words came from
We collected these terms in a loop:

Search with the words we already had.
Read the titles and abstracts of the results.
Add any new names for the idea to the list.
Search again with the new words.

The loop stops when new searches return only papers already in the log. In our search, the first query used the words “algebra,” “bookkeeping,” and “double-entry.” The term “Pacioli group” came from the abstract of the first relevant paper, and “bookkeeping graphs” came from a later query that added “graph theory.”

title: 3  Finding the First Paper
text:
3.1 The first query
A literature search needs a starting point: one paper that is on topic. From that paper you can follow references and citations (Chapter 4). This chapter shows how we found ours and how we checked its bibliographic data.
Our first search used a general web search engine with the query
The filetype:pdf part asks for PDF files, and all but one of the results we received were PDFs. Among the results was a PDF of Ellerman (1985) on the author’s own website, and a PDF of Ellerman (2014) on arXiv. Both are by the same author. The abstract of Ellerman (2014) describes bookkeeping in terms of a group, which matched our first question in Chapter 1. We chose Ellerman (2014) as the starting paper because it is the more recent of the two. A recent paper is a good start because its reference list can lead back to earlier work.

title: 3  Finding the First Paper
text:
3.3 Checking the bibliographic data
A search result is a pointer to a paper, and the details it shows can be incomplete. Before a reference enters the bibliography of this book, we check it against a record kept by the publisher or by a registry.

arXiv. The arXiv API returns the title, authors, abstract, subject category, and first submission date of a preprint. We queried it with au:Ellerman AND abs:bookkeeping and received exactly one record, arXiv:1407.1898.
Crossref. We sent each journal article and conference paper in this book’s bibliography, as free text, to Crossref’s public API (api.crossref.org/works with the query.bibliographic parameter). It returned the closest registered records with their DOI, journal, volume, issue, pages, and date.

The Crossref result is only a candidate. Compare it with the reference you are checking: same authors, same title, same year. Chapter 9 shows a case where the best match was a different record.

title: 4  Following Citations
text:
4.1 Backward and forward
Once you have one good paper, the papers connected to it lead to the rest of the literature. This chapter covers three ways to follow those connections: by hand through references and citations, with a similarity graph, and with a scholarly database API.
A paper connects to the literature in two directions.
Google Scholar’s search help gives a rule of thumb for choosing a direction. If your results are too specific, look at the works they cite, which tend to be more general. If your results are too basic, look at the papers that cite them, which tend to be newer and more specific.
We repeated both steps from each new relevant paper. Wohlin (2014) gives guidelines for conducting literature reviews with a snowballing approach, evaluates them by replicating a published systematic review, and concludes that snowballing can be a good alternative to database searches as a first search strategy.

title: 4  Following Citations
text:
Backward: the works it cites, listed in its references. These are older.
Forward: the later works that cite it. Google Scholar shows these under “Cited by.”

section: 4.3 Database APIs: Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex
text:
4.3 Database APIs: Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex
For larger searches, a program can follow citations for you through a database API.

Semantic Scholar offers the Academic Graph API. Most endpoints work without an API key, but unauthenticated requests share a rate limit of 1,000 requests per second across all such users and may be throttled further when traffic is heavy. A personal API key starts with a limit of one request per second.
OpenAlex describes itself as a free and open catalog of the world’s scholarly research system. Its data is released under the CC0 license and is available through an API and as a bulk download.

When we sent unauthenticated search requests to the Semantic Scholar API on 15 October 2026, it answered “Too Many Requests.” Chapter 9 returns to this.

title: 5  Searching Literature in Japanese
text:
5.1 The databases
Part of the work on the algebra of bookkeeping is written in Japanese. The papers in this chapter appeared in a university bulletin and are available from a university repository. This chapter introduces the Japanese databases we used and shows how their results differed.

title: 5  Searching Literature in Japanese
text:
CiNii Research, run by the National Institute of Informatics (NII), searches several kinds of records from one box: data, articles, books, dissertations, research projects, and researchers.
IRDB (Institutional Repositories DataBase) is also run by NII. As its name says, it is a database of institutional repositories.
J-STAGE is a platform for scholarly publications in Japan, developed and managed by the Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST). Its overview page lists more than 4,000 journals, proceedings, and other publications from more than 2,400 publishers in Japan.
NDL Search, run by the National Diet Library, searches the library’s own printed and digital holdings. It also searches bibliographic and location information for books held by prefectural and municipal libraries, and materials from university and specialty libraries and research institutions across Japan.

title: 5  Searching Literature in Japanese
section: 5.2 A worked example: one term, two tools
text:
5.2 A worked example: one term, two tools
The Japanese term 簿記代数 (“bookkeeping algebra”) came from our keyword loop (Chapter 2): a Google Scholar query in Japanese (簿記 代数 構造 OR 複式簿記 数学 群) returned a paper whose title contains it. On 15 October 2026 we then searched two tools.
CiNii Research. A search for 簿記代数 across all record types returned one result: Ozawa (2023a), published in 2023 in the bulletin 商学研究科紀要, no. 97, pp. 79–96.
Google Scholar. A search for the author of that paper together with 複式簿記 (“double-entry bookkeeping”) returned three papers by this author with PDFs in the Waseda University repository: Ozawa (2023a), Ozawa (2023b), and Ozawa (2026). It also listed one co-authored paper without a PDF. The title of the 2026 paper refers to a monoid structure of records and a group structure of net balances, the distinction that this book develops in Part IV.
The two tools returned different sets. The CiNii search used one term, and only one of the three titles contains that exact term. The Scholar search used the author’s name. A single query in a single database is a sample of the literature, and the log should record which query produced which result.

title: 6  Finding Older Literature
text:
6.1 Digitized books: the Internet Archive
The oldest work in this book’s bibliography was written in 1880. Finding and checking work that old took us different tools and more steps than finding recent papers.
The Internet Archive holds scanned copies of old books, including the one discussed in this section. It offers an advanced search that returns results as JSON, so a search can be logged exactly. We queried it for books with “philosophy of accounts” in the title and “Sprague” as creator. It returned eight records of The Philosophy of Accounts by Charles Ezra Sprague (1842–1912), dated 1908, 1920, 1922, and 1972. This book cites the 1908 scan (Sprague 1908).
When a book exists in several editions, record which edition you read. Page numbers and even content can change between editions.

title: 6  Finding Older Literature
text:
6.2 A nineteenth-century article
Several modern papers cite a series of articles by Sprague titled “The Algebra of Accounts” from 1880. Our Internet Archive search did not return the 1880 issues of the periodical, but the articles were reprinted in a collection edited by Richard Brief, first published in 1982 and reissued in 2013 (Brief 2013). The Internet Archive’s catalog record for the 1982 edition lists Sprague’s “The algebra of accounts” among its contents. In the publisher’s table of contents for the 2013 reissue, the chapter carries the note that it was written for The Book-keeper. This book cites the reprint (Sprague 2013).
The same publisher page also shows how catalog data can go wrong. It lists the chapter’s author as “Charles E. Spraoue,” credits two other chapters to the editor instead of their authors, and shows a description that belongs to a different book on depreciation. Take the facts you need from the reprinted text and from more than one record.

title: 6  Finding Older Literature
text:
6.3 History papers as guides
Papers on the history of accounting can point to older primary sources. Two that our searches found have titles that match this book’s themes:

Peters and Emery (1978), on the role of negative numbers in the development of double-entry bookkeeping;
Stone (2021), on the connection between Luca Pacioli, algebra, and double entry.

Part XIV returns to them.

title: 7  Reading Papers
text:
7.1 Read in passes
A search produces more papers than anyone can read in full. You need a way to decide quickly which papers matter, and a way to read the ones that do.
Keshav (2007) describes a practical three-pass method for reading research papers and explains how to use it for a literature survey. This book borrows the structure of reading a paper more than once, with each pass deciding whether the next is worth the time. Our passes are adapted for mathematical papers, and their details are ours.
The first pass exists to filter, so expect most papers to stop there.

title: 7  Reading Papers
text:
Survey. Read the title, abstract, section headings, and conclusion. Decide whether the paper answers one of your questions from Chapter 1.
Statements. Read every definition and every theorem statement, and skip the proofs. Write each definition in your own notation.
Proofs. Read the proofs of the results you will use. Check each step, or formalize it.

title: 7  Reading Papers
text:
7.2 Extracting the main claim
After the first pass, write the paper’s main claim in one or two sentences, using only what the paper says. For Ellerman (2014) the abstract gives us the following.

Double-entry bookkeeping implicitly uses a specific mathematical construction: the group of differences built from pairs of unsigned numbers, which the paper calls the Pacioli group.
This construction was formulated abstractly in mathematics only in the nineteenth century, although bookkeeping had used it for centuries.
A precise mathematical treatment yields a generalization of double entry to multi-dimensional vectors, which typically represent the different types of property in an enterprise or a household.

Each sentence above restates the abstract. None of them adds a claim the abstract does not make. When a summary goes beyond the source, mark the extra part as your own interpretation.

title: 7  Reading Papers
section: 7.3 Reading a paper in a field you do not know
text:
7.3 Reading a paper in a field you do not know
Papers on the algebra of bookkeeping come from accounting, mathematics, and computer science. A mathematician may not know what a “trial balance” is, and an accountant may not know what a “group of differences” is. Keep a two-column glossary in your log: the term as the paper uses it, and its meaning in the other field. Part II of this book introduces the bookkeeping terms, and the glossary in the appendix pairs them with their mathematical counterparts.

title: 8  Organizing What You Find
text:
8.1 The research log
A search that is not recorded has to be repeated. This chapter covers three records worth keeping: the research log, the bibliography file, and a map of research lines.
The log records each search as it happens: date, tool, exact query, number of results, and the papers kept. It also has a place for references that are not yet checked (Chapter 6).

title: 8  Organizing What You Find
text:
8.2 The bibliography file
This book stores references in a BibTeX file, references.bib. Quarto, the system used to build this book, generates citations and the bibliography through Pandoc. It needs a document with citations, a bibliographic data source such as a BibLaTeX or BibTeX file, and, optionally, a CSL file that sets the citation style. A document names its bibliography in its YAML header, for example bibliography: references.bib, and cites an entry by its key, for example [@ellerman2014].
Each entry in this book’s file was checked before it was added (Chapter 3). The file contains only bibliographic fields: authors, title, venue, volume, issue, pages, year, and DOI. A field that we could not check is left out, even when a search snippet showed a value for it.

title: 9  Limits and Pitfalls
text:
9.1 Usage limits
Several tools in Part 0 failed us at least once. This chapter records those failures, because a reader who repeats our search may meet the same ones.
Connected Papers. The free plan allows five graphs per month; the paid plans allow unlimited graphs. In our session, the first two graphs loaded. When we then requested graphs for Arya et al. (2000) and for a work titled Momentum Accounting and Triple Entry Bookkeeping: Exploring the Dynamic Structure of Accounting Measurements, the page asked us to log in and reported that the monthly graph limit had been reached. We did not see those two graphs.
Semantic Scholar API. Unauthenticated requests share one rate limit across all unauthenticated users (Chapter 4). Our unauthenticated search requests on 15 October 2026 were refused with the message “Too Many Requests,” which suggests requesting an API key.
Crossref API. Some of our requests from the browser were refused with HTTP status 429, which signals too many requests. The same queries succeeded later from the command line.
Record each limit in the log, then continue with another tool. After the Semantic Scholar refusal we continued with Google Scholar.

title: 9  Limits and Pitfalls
text:
9.2 Gaps in documentation
We looked for a description of Google Scholar’s author: search operator in its search help page and did not find one there. Part 0 therefore teaches only the Scholar features we found documented: sorting by date, “Cited by,” “Related articles,” “All versions,” and following a paper’s references.

title: 9  Limits and Pitfalls
section: 9.3 A registry match that was a different record
text:
9.3 A registry match that was a different record
When we sent the citation of Ijiri’s 1965 paper to Crossref, the best match had the right title and author but was a 2018 reprint in the journal Accounting, Economics, and Law: A Convivium. A reader who copied that record would cite the wrong year and the wrong journal. Restricting the query to works published before 1967 returned the original in The Accounting Review (Ijiri 1965), but that record spells the author’s name “Tjiri.” Compare every field of a registry match with your source before you accept it (Chapter 3).

title: 9  Limits and Pitfalls
section: 9.4 Copies from sites that are not the publisher
text:
9.4 Copies from sites that are not the publisher
General web searches return PDFs from many kinds of sites. Our second web query returned a PDF of a book on accounting history from a document-sharing site. We could not establish that the site had the right to distribute the book, so this book does not use that copy. Use the publisher’s version, an author’s copy, a preprint server, or a library.

title: 9  Limits and Pitfalls
text:
9.5 Fabricated references from chatbots
Walters and Wilder (2023) asked ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 to write short literature reviews on 42 topics and checked the 636 references in the 84 resulting papers. They report that 55% of the GPT-3.5 references and 18% of the GPT-4 references were fabricated, that is, they did not correspond to any real work. Among the references to real works, 43% from GPT-3.5 and 24% from GPT-4 contained substantive citation errors.
A language model can help to brainstorm search terms. It cannot replace a check against the source. Every reference in this book was checked against the source, a registry record, or an archive record.

title: 9  Limits and Pitfalls
text:
9.6 Our own near-misses
The rules in this part come partly from mistakes we caught while writing it.

We first wrote that a search restricted to the English term “double-entry” would miss the category theory paper Katis et al. (2008). The Scholar search log showed that a query containing “double-entry” did return it. We corrected the text in Chapter 2.
We first romanized the Japanese titles in the bibliography without checking their readings. We replaced the romanizations with the original titles and marked our translations (Chapter 5).
We first listed Nehmer and Robinson (1997) among the neighbors of Ellerman (2014) in the Connected Papers graph. It appeared in a different graph. We corrected Chapter 4.

We caught each error by comparing the text with the records of our searches.

The works in the timeline apply different areas of mathematics to bookkeeping: groups, algebraic models and automata, matrices, graphs, and categories.
